questions.stem: A 71-year-old man presented with a 5-month history of drainage from his right total hip arthroplasty (THA) incision (completed 3 years prior). There were associated lowgrade fevers, increasing fatigue, and lack of appetite. He was known to have hypertension, asthma, and depression. He was allergic to sulfa drugs, with previous anaphylaxis. On examination, there was a sinus tract over the right hip with surrounding cellulitis. Investigations: X-ray of the right hip demonstrated periprosthetic lucency. Blood cultures: MRSA sensitive to trimethoprim–sulfamethoxazole (TMP–SMX), linezolid, and vancomycin; resistant to clindamycin and doxycycline
questions.lead_in: What is the most appropriate surgical intervention?
questions.explanation: Two-stage exchange Given the presence of a late prosthetic joint infection (onset >24 months after surgery), prolonged duration of symptoms, and presence of sinus tract on physical exam, a DAIR would not be recommended given the risk for relapse of infection, especially in the setting of MRSA infection. With DAIR and one-stage exchange, a period of oral antibiotic suppression is required following completion of parenteral therapy. The patient as described above does not have any viable oral antibiotic options given the isolate’s susceptibility pattern and his allergy history. While the isolate is sensitive to linezolid, it is not an ideal antibiotic for long-term use given the potential for hematologic toxicity associated with >14 days of therapy (most commonly, thrombocytopenia) as well as rare adverse events (lactic acidosis, optic neuritis, and peripheral neuropathy). Additionally, the patient has a history of depression, to which selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs), and tricyclic antidepressants (TCAs) can pose significant drug–drug interactions with linezolid use. Given the nature of his infection, the patient’s allergy history, and comorbidities, a twostage exchange would be ideally employed in this scenario.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 2 Q24

questions.question: Regarding the management of prosthetic joint infection, what are 5 criteria that must be met for a patient to be considered appropriate for management with a debridement and implant-retention strategy?
questions.question_raw: 8. Regarding the management of PJI, what are 5 criteria that must be met for a patient to be considered appropriate for management with a debridement/retention strategy?

parts.text: What are 5 criteria that must be met for a patient to be considered appropriate for management with a debridement/retention strategy?

parts_raw.text: What are 5 criteria that must be met for a patient to be considered appropriate for management with a debridement/retention strategy?

questions.model_answer: a) (1) Acute infection — symptom duration less than 3 weeks, or within 1 month (up to 4 weeks) of implantation, or acute hematogenous infection after an uneventful postoperative course. (2) Stable, well-fixed implant. (3) Pathogen susceptible to an antimicrobial active against surface-adhering (biofilm) organisms — e.g. rifampin for staphylococci, a fluoroquinolone for gram-negative bacilli. (4) No sinus tract and no periprosthetic abscess. (5) Intact or only slightly damaged soft tissue envelope (otherwise exchange is required). Open rather than arthroscopic debridement with exchange of modular components is required.

cohort_answer.text: Well-fixed prosthesis; absence of sinus tract; within 30 days of placement; <3 weeks of symptoms; good oral suppression options available

questions.question: Selection of debridement and implant retention rather than two-stage exchange in knee prosthetic joint infection.

parts.text: What are 5 indications for using debridement and retention strategy over two stage exchange in knee PJI?

parts_raw.text: What are 5 indications for using debridement and retention strategy over two stage exchange in knee PJI?

questions.model_answer: a) (1) Acute infection: less than 3 weeks of symptoms, or within 1 month of implantation, or acute hematogenous infection after an uneventful postoperative course. (2) Implant stable and well fixed (no loosening). (3) Causative pathogen susceptible to a biofilm-active antimicrobial (rifampin combination for staphylococci; fluoroquinolone for gram-negative bacilli) — not a difficult-to-treat organism. (4) Absence of a sinus tract and absence of a periprosthetic abscess. (5) Intact or only slightly damaged soft tissue envelope, permitting thorough open debridement with exchange of modular components.

questions.question: Prosthetic knee infection.

parts.text: List 5 criteria to determine whether it is appropriate to do retention of hardware.

parts_raw.text: List 5 criteria to determine whether it is appropriate to do retention of hardware. (2.5 points)

questions.model_answer: a) (1) Acute infection: symptoms less than 3 weeks, or within 1 month of implantation, or acute hematogenous infection after an uneventful course. (2) Implant stable and well fixed. (3) Organism susceptible to a biofilm-active antimicrobial (rifampin-susceptible staphylococci; fluoroquinolone-susceptible gram-negative bacilli) — no difficult-to-treat pathogen. (4) No sinus tract and no periprosthetic abscess. (5) Intact or only slightly damaged soft tissue, allowing thorough open debridement with exchange of modular components (open debridement success ~86% vs ~56% arthroscopic in knee PJI).

questions.question: A previously well 10-year-old boy fell 11 months ago and broke his humerus. He had open reduction and internal fixation but had ongoing pain for months. Four months ago the pins were removed because of the pain. He now presents with ongoing pain. [image-based question: 2 X-rays of the shoulder shown]
questions.question_raw: 10 yo boy previously well. Fell 11 months ago and broke humerus. Had ORIF but ongoing pain for months. 4 months ago, the pins were removed because of the pain. Now presents with ongoing pain. [image-based question: 2 X-rays of the shoulder shown]
questions.model_answer: a) Chronic implant (fracture-fixation)–associated osteomyelitis of the humerus — a delayed/late internal fixation device infection persisting after hardware removal, with radiographic chronic osteomyelitis (lytic/sclerotic change, periosteal new bone, sequestrum/ring sequestrum at the former pin tracts) and infected nonunion.

parts.text: What is the most likely organism (genus, species)?
What would be the optimal surgical management for this condition?
Name 2 antibiotics this organism is usually susceptible to.

parts_raw.text: What is the most likely organism (genus, species)?
What would be the optimal surgical management for this condition?
Name 2 antibiotics this organism is usually susceptible to.

questions.model_answer:
a) Cutibacterium acnes (formerly Propionibacterium acnes) — anaerobic gram-positive rod, the classic low-virulence pathogen of shoulder periprosthetic infection (up to 38% of periprosthetic shoulder infections); requires prolonged culture incubation (10-14 days).
b) Prosthesis exchange, not debridement with retention: this is a delayed presentation (>1 month after implantation, symptoms >3 weeks), so the implant must be removed. Two-stage exchange (removal of all foreign material and necrotic tissue, antibiotic-impregnated spacer, reimplantation — short 2-3-week interval if soft tissue is intact and the organism is not difficult to treat), with a one-stage exchange acceptable when the soft tissue envelope is good and the organism is susceptible to a highly bioavailable oral agent; cure rates in shoulder PJI are 90%-92% with either approach.
c) (1) Penicillin G (with oral step-down amoxicillin). (2) Clindamycin.

cohort_answer.text: Organism: Cutibacterium acnes. Bacteriology note: Joint revision surgery samples require extended incubation, up to 14 days. Surgical management: Removal of hardware (typically unable to eradicate infection unless this occurs); 2-stage exchange; Antibiotics according to type of procedure. Indications for 2 stage exchange: Poor soft tissue; Difficult to treat microorganism; Patient unable to undergo 1 stage; Medically stable for multiple surgeries; Reimplantation prosthesis possible; Anticipate good functional outcome. Antibiotics: Susceptible to beta lactams - Penicillin, Cephalosporins, Carbapenems, Clindamycin. NB. Propionibacterium resistant to flagyl, may be resistant to tetracyclines and macrolides.

questions.question: Biofilms and their role in infection.

parts.text: Name four infections associated with them.
Why do they make bacteria resistant to killing?

parts_raw.text: Why do they make bacteria resistant to killing?

questions.model_answer:
a) (1) Cardiovascular implantable electronic device (CIED) infection. (2) Prosthetic vascular graft infection. (3) Left ventricular assist device (LVAD) infection. (4) Infective endocarditis (native/prosthetic valve). (Other valid: prosthetic joint infection, intravascular catheter infection.)
b) Biofilm is a protective extracellular slime matrix that impairs eradication by: poor penetration of antibiotics into the biofilm; downregulated metabolic activity/dormancy of the embedded organisms making them less susceptible to antimicrobials; and impaired host defense (neutrophil dysfunction) - which is why device removal is usually required for cure.

cohort_answer.text: Infections: PJI, IE, Vascular graft infections, diabetic foot infections and dental caries, CF infections. Resistance: Significantly increases the effective MIC by preventing adequate delivery of antibiotic to the organism.

questions.question_raw: Patient with shoulder arthroplasty 5 months ago now presents with infection of that same shoulder. The pathogen grows on anaerobic plates only. Shown a photo of Gram stain from shoulder aspirate, messy looking GPB.

parts.text: What is the surgical treatment of choice?
Name two antibiotics to which it is susceptible.

parts_raw.text: What is the surgical treatment of choice?
Name two antibiotics to which it is susceptible.

questions.model_answer:
a) Cutibacterium acnes (formerly Propionibacterium acnes) — slow-growing anaerobic gram-positive rod needing 10-14 days of incubation; causes up to 38% of periprosthetic shoulder infections.
b) Two-stage exchange arthroplasty: removal of all implant material, cement and necrotic tissue with insertion of an antibiotic-loaded spacer, then reimplantation (short 2-3-week interval since C. acnes is not a difficult-to-treat organism). Debridement with retention is not appropriate at 5 months with a delayed presentation.
c) (1) Penicillin G (oral step-down amoxicillin). (2) Clindamycin. (Metronidazole is inactive against Cutibacterium.)

cohort_answer.text: Cutibacterium acnes (usually grows at 5-7 days, strong association with shoulder arthroplasty failure). Surgical treatment: Two-stage revision. Susceptible antibiotics: Penicillins, Vancomycin, Linezolid (also ceftriaxone); no breakpoints for cefazolin; resistant to metronidazole

Their other drugs are: hydrochlorothiazide, ASA, bisoprolol, perindopril, calcium, metformin, vitamin D, rivaroxaban, sertraline, vitamin B12, amlodipine. In a table, list 4 possible drug interactions, with the antibiotic in the first column, the other drug in the second, and the interaction in the third.

Their other drugs are: HCTZ, ASA, Bisoprolol, Perindopril, Calcium, Metformin, Vitamin D, Rivaroxaban, Sertraline, Vitamin B12, amlodipine. In a table, list 4 possible drug interactions, with ABx in first column, other drug in second, and interaction in 3rd.

parts.text: List 4 possible drug interactions (antibiotic, other drug, interaction).

parts_raw.text: List 4 possible drug interactions (antibiotic, other drug, interaction)

questions.model_answer: (1) Rifampin | rivaroxaban - rifampin induces CYP3A4/P-glycoprotein, decreasing rivaroxaban concentration and anticoagulant effect. (2) Rifampin | amlodipine (or bisoprolol) - CYP3A4 induction lowers the calcium-channel/beta-blocker level, reducing antihypertensive efficacy. (3) Ciprofloxacin | calcium - polyvalent cation chelation reduces ciprofloxacin absorption (separate dosing). (4) Linezolid | sertraline - additive serotonergic effect (linezolid is a weak MAO inhibitor); risk of serotonin syndrome.
questions.beyond_mandell: Ciprofloxacin-calcium chelation and linezolid-sertraline serotonin syndrome are established pharmacology; the rifamycin chapter lists rivaroxaban, calcium-channel blockers, beta-blockers and linezolid among rifampin interactions (Table 27.2) but does not detail the non-rifampin mechanisms.

cohort_answer.text: Rifampin-Rivaroxaban: CYP3A4 strong inducers may decrease serum concentration of rivaroxaban. Rifampin-Sertraline: CYP3A4 strong inducers may decrease serum concentration of sertraline. Rifampin-Bisoprolol/Perindopril/Amlodipine: CYP3A4 strong inducers may decrease serum concentration. Linezolid-Metformin: MAOIs may enhance hypoglycemic effect. Linezolid-Sertraline: linezolid may enhance serotonergic effect of SSRIs, risk of serotonin syndrome. Ciprofloxacin-Metformin: quinolones may enhance/diminish hypoglycemic effect. Ciprofloxacin-Calcium: multivitamins/minerals may decrease serum concentration of quinolones (polyvalent cations decrease absorption). Also caution with QT-prolonging agents.

questions.question_raw: Prosthetic shoulder inflamed 7 months after surgery (didn't mention how long symptoms). Aspirated, showed a picture of GPB growing anaerobically.
questions.model_answer:
a) Cutibacterium acnes (formerly Propionibacterium acnes).
b) Two-stage exchange: removal of the prosthesis, cement and all necrotic tissue, insertion of an antibiotic-impregnated (PMMA) spacer, antimicrobial therapy, then reimplantation of a new prosthesis at a second procedure (short 2-3-week interval unless soft tissue is damaged or the organism is difficult to treat; one-stage exchange is an alternative with a good soft tissue envelope and a highly bioavailable oral agent). Retention is not an option at this delayed stage.
c) (1) Penicillin G (or oral amoxicillin). (2) Clindamycin.

cohort_answer.text: Cutibacterium acnes. Surgical management: 2 stage exchange - hardware removal, debridement, insert cement spacer, treat with antibiotics, then reinsert hardware at second stage. Effective drugs: Penicillin, Clindamycin, Vanco, Carbapenems (resistant to Flagyl)

questions.question: Biofilms.

parts.text: Name four situations where biofilm can form that do not involve prosthetic material.

parts_raw.text: A) Name 4 situations where there can be biofilm formation, not involving prosthetic material?

questions.model_answer: a) (1) Infective endocarditis (native valve vegetations). (2) Cystic fibrosis airway infection (Pseudomonas aeruginosa). (3) Chronic otitis media. (4) Dental caries/periodontitis (oral cavity). (Other valid: chronic bacterial prostatitis, chronic wound infections.)
questions.beyond_mandell: Non-device biofilm settings are not enumerated in this device-focused chapter; answer based on established microbiology knowledge.

cohort_answer.text: Infective endocarditis; Wound infections; Cystic fibrosis; Otitis media; Oral cavity/dental caries, periodontitis; Chronic bacterial prostatitis (speaker notes: CF, PICC Line, endocarditis, pseudo)
